claim: Over 1000 proteins are utilized by mitochondria to perform their functions.
source: Although over 1000 proteins are utilized by mitochondria to perform their functions, only ~1% of them are synthesized inside this organelle.
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge about mitochondrial protein composition.

claim: Only approximately 1% of mitochondrial proteins are synthesized inside the organelle.
source: Although over 1000 proteins are utilized by mitochondria to perform their functions, only ~1% of them are synthesized inside this organelle.
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge about mitochondrial protein synthesis.

claim: The majority of mitochondrial proteins are synthesized in the cytosol and need to be actively transported to mitochondria.
source: The majority of mitochondrial proteins are synthesized in the cytosol and need to be actively transported to mitochondria, a process that occurs via a sophisticated system that involves protein translocases and sorting machineries (Calvo et al., 2016; Morgenstern et al., 2017; Neupert and Herrmann, 2007; Pfanner et al., 2019).
evidence: This statement is supported by multiple citations to prior research.

claim: Mitochondrial protein import occurs via a sophisticated system that involves protein translocases and sorting machineries.
source: The majority of mitochondrial proteins are synthesized in the cytosol and need to be actively transported to mitochondria, a process that occurs via a sophisticated system that involves protein translocases and sorting machineries (Calvo et al., 2016; Morgenstern et al., 2017; Neupert and Herrmann, 2007; Pfanner et al., 2019).
evidence: This is supported by citations to established research on mitochondrial protein import.

claim: The consequences of mitochondrial protein import defects on cellular proteostasis can be severe.
source: The consequences of mitochondrial protein import defects on cellular proteostasis can be severe, and currently some response mechanisms are identified (Boos et al., 2019; Izawa et al., 2017; Kim et al., 2016; Martensson et al., 2019; Priesnitz and Becker, 2018; Wang and Chen, 2015; Weidberg and Amon, 2018; Wrobel et al., 2015; Wu et al., 2019; Poveda-Huertes et al., 2020).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations to prior research on mitochondrial import defects.

claim: Mitochondrial dysfunction is closely associated with neurodegenerative disorders.
source: Mitochondrial dysfunction is closely associated with neurodegenerative disorders, and such mitochondrial defects as aberrant Ca2+ handling, increases in reactive oxygen species, electron transport chain inhibition, and impairments in endoplasmic reticulum-mitochondria tethering are well-described pathological markers (Cabral-Costa and Kowaltowski, 2020).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to prior research on mitochondrial dysfunction in neurodegeneration.

claim: Aberrant Ca2+ handling, increases in reactive oxygen species, electron transport chain inhibition, and impairments in endoplasmic reticulum-mitochondria tethering are well-described pathological markers of mitochondrial dysfunction.
source: Mitochondrial dysfunction is closely associated with neurodegenerative disorders, and such mitochondrial defects as aberrant Ca2+ handling, increases in reactive oxygen species, electron transport chain inhibition, and impairments in endoplasmic reticulum-mitochondria tethering are well-described pathological markers (Cabral-Costa and Kowaltowski, 2020).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to prior research.

claim: Disease-related proteins can interfere with mitochondrial import and the further processing of imported proteins within mitochondria.
source: Disease-related proteins can interfere with mitochondrial import and the further processing of imported proteins within mitochondria (Cenini et al., 2016; Di Maio et al., 2016; Mossmann et al., 2014; Vicario et al., 2018).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations to prior research.

claim: Aggregated proteins can be imported into mitochondria where they can be either cleared or sequestered in specific deposit sites.
source: Furthermore, aggregated proteins can be imported into mitochondria where they can be either cleared or sequestered in specific deposit sites (Bruderek et al., 2018; Ruan et al., 2017; Sorrentino et al., 2017).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations to prior research.

claim: Impairments in mitochondrial protein import and mitochondrial import machinery overload result in the accumulation of mitochondria-targeted proteins in the cytosol.
source: Impairments in mitochondrial protein import and mitochondrial import machinery overload result in the accumulation of mitochondria-targeted proteins in the cytosol and stimulation of mitoprotein-induced stress (Boos et al., 2019; Wang and Chen, 2015; Wrobel et al., 2015).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations to prior research.

claim: Impairments in mitochondrial protein import stimulate mitoprotein-induced stress.
source: Impairments in mitochondrial protein import and mitochondrial import machinery overload result in the accumulation of mitochondria-targeted proteins in the cytosol and stimulation of mitoprotein-induced stress (Boos et al., 2019; Wang and Chen, 2015; Wrobel et al., 2015).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations to prior research.

claim: The analysis of a transcriptional signature of Alzheimer's disease supports the notion that there is a subset of mitochondrial proteins that is more dangerous than others for the cell.
source: The analysis of a transcriptional signature of Alzheimer's disease supports the notion that there is a subset of mitochondrial proteins that is more dangerous than others for the cell (Ciryam et al., 2016; Kundra et al., 2017).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior research.

claim: Specific mitochondrial proteins that are functionally related to oxidative phosphorylation are transcriptionally downregulated in Alzheimer's disease.
source: These studies have shown that specific mitochondrial proteins that are functionally related to oxidative phosphorylation are transcriptionally downregulated in Alzheimer's disease.
evidence: This is stated as a finding from prior studies referenced in the previous sentence.

claim: When some mitochondrial proteins remain in the cytosol because of mitochondrial protein import insufficiency, they formed insoluble aggregates that disrupted protein homeostasis.
source: Our results showed that when some of these mitochondrial proteins remain in the cytosol because of mitochondrial protein import insufficiency, they formed insoluble aggregates that disrupted protein homeostasis.
evidence: This is stated as a result from the current study.

claim: Mitochondrial protein aggregates triggered a prompt-specific molecular chaperone response that aimed to minimize the consequences of protein aggregation.
source: These proteins triggered a prompt-specific molecular chaperone response that aimed to minimize the consequences of protein aggregation.
evidence: This is stated as a result from the current study.

claim: When the molecular chaperone rescue mechanism was insufficient, mitochondrial protein aggregates stimulated the cytosolic aggregation of other mitochondrial proteins.
source: However, when this rescue mechanism was insufficient, these aggregates stimulated the cytosolic aggregation of other mitochondrial proteins and led to the downstream aggregation of non-mitochondrial proteins.
evidence: This is stated as a result from the current study.

claim: Mitochondrial protein aggregates led to the downstream aggregation of non-mitochondrial proteins.
source: However, when this rescue mechanism was insufficient, these aggregates stimulated the cytosolic aggregation of other mitochondrial proteins and led to the downstream aggregation of non-mitochondrial proteins.
evidence: This is stated as a result from the current study.

claim: Metastable mitochondrial proteins can be transcriptionally downregulated during neurodegeneration to minimize cellular protein homeostasis imbalance that is caused by their mistargeting.
source: Our findings indicate that metastable mitochondrial proteins can be transcriptionally downregulated during neurodegeneration to minimize cellular protein homeostasis imbalance that is caused by their mistargeting.
evidence: This is stated as an interpretation of the study's findings.

claim: Oxidative phosphorylation is a pathway that is metastable and downregulated in the human central nervous system in Alzheimer's disease.
source: The analysis of a transcriptomic signature of Alzheimer's disease identified oxidative phosphorylation as a pathway that is metastable and downregulated in the human central nervous system (Ciryam et al., 2016; Kundra et al., 2017).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior research.

claim: The β and g subunits of mitochondrial F1FO adenosine triphosphate (ATP) synthase (Atp2 and Atp20, respectively) were present in the insoluble fraction, indicating that they formed high-molecular-weight deposits.
source: We found that the β and g subunits of mitochondrial F1FO adenosine triphosphate (ATP) synthase (Atp2 and Atp20, respectively) were present in the insoluble fraction, indicating that they formed high-molecular-weight deposits (Figure 1A, Figure 1—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in figures.

claim: Rip1 and Cox8 had entirely insoluble precursor (p) forms.
source: Rip1 and subunit VIII of cytochrome c oxidase complex IV (Cox8) had entirely insoluble precursor (p) forms, whereas the mature (m) forms were partially insoluble (the p form of the protein is larger and migrates on the gel above the m form; Figure 1A, Figure 1—figure supplement 1C).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in figures.

claim: The mature forms of Rip1 and Cox8 were partially insoluble.
source: Rip1 and subunit VIII of cytochrome c oxidase complex IV (Cox8) had entirely insoluble precursor (p) forms, whereas the mature (m) forms were partially insoluble (the p form of the protein is larger and migrates on the gel above the m form; Figure 1A, Figure 1—figure supplement 1C).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in figures.

claim: The mature forms of Qcr8, Cor1, and Mas1 were partially insoluble.
source: Furthermore, the mature forms of subunit VIII of ubiquinol cytochrome c reductase complex III (Qcr8), core subunit of the ubiquinol-cytochrome c reductase complex (Cor1), and subunit β of the mitochondrial processing protease (MPP; Mas1) were partially insoluble.
evidence: This is stated as a result from the current study.

claim: Cox12 and Qcr6 were mainly present in the soluble fraction.
source: Only subunit VIb of cytochrome c oxidase (Cox12) and subunit 6 of ubiquinol cytochrome c reductase complex (Qcr6) were mainly present in the soluble fraction (Figure 1A, Figure 1—figure supplement 1C).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in figures.

claim: The tendency to aggregate and its harmful consequences correlated well with growth defects of yeast transformants that overexpressed mitochondrial proteins.
source: Moreover, the tendency to aggregate and its harmful consequences correlated well with growth defects of yeast transformants that overexpressed mitochondrial proteins (Figure 1B, Figure 1—figure supplement 1D).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in figures.

claim: The higher amount of an overproduced protein in the insoluble fraction correlated with a greater increase in lethality.
source: We observed that the higher amount of an overproduced protein in the insoluble fraction correlated with a greater increase in lethality.
evidence: This is stated as an observation from the current study.

claim: The general molecular chaperone response that was associated with an increase in temperature did not compensate for the observed changes for Atp2, Cox8, or pRip1.
source: This difference was still present under heat shock conditions of 37°C, indicating that the general molecular chaperone response that was associated with an increase in temperature did not compensate for the observed changes for Atp2, Cox8, or pRip1 and could only partially compensate for Cox12 and Atp20.
evidence: This is stated as an observation from the current study.

claim: The general molecular chaperone response that was associated with an increase in temperature could only partially compensate for Cox12 and Atp20.
source: This difference was still present under heat shock conditions of 37°C, indicating that the general molecular chaperone response that was associated with an increase in temperature did not compensate for the observed changes for Atp2, Cox8, or pRip1 and could only partially compensate for Cox12 and Atp20.
evidence: This is stated as an observation from the current study.

claim: Mitochondrial import defects triggered either chemically or by mutations of the TIM23 translocase resulted in the accumulation and aggregation of mitochondrial precursor proteins.
source: Our study demonstrated that mitochondrial import defects, triggered either chemically or by mutations of the TIM23 translocase, resulted in the accumulation and aggregation of mitochondrial precursor proteins.
evidence: This is stated as a result from the current study.

claim: Cells treated with CCCP had a compromised mitochondrial inner membrane (IM) electrochemical potential and protein import failure.
source: Consistent with previous studies (Wrobel et al., 2015), cells that were treated with the chemical uncoupler carbonyl cyanide m-chlorophenyl hydrazine (CCCP) had a compromised mitochondrial inner membrane (IM) electrochemical potential and protein import failure (Chacinska et al., 2009; Neupert and Herrmann, 2007; van der Laan et al., 2010).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior research.

claim: Perturbations of IM potential resulted in the accumulation of p forms of Rip1 (pRip1).
source: Perturbations of IM potential resulted in the accumulation of p forms of Rip1 (pRip1), similar to when the full precursor form of Rip1 was overproduced (Figure 1C and D, Figure 1—figure supplement 1E).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in figures.

claim: The accumulation of pRip1, pSod2, and pMdh1 increased as CCCP concentrations increased.
source: The accumulation of pRip1, the p form of Sod2 (pSod2), and the p form of Mdh1 (pMdh1) increased as CCCP concentrations increased (Figure 1C and D).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in figures.

claim: pRip, pSod2, and pMdh1 were present in the pellet fractions, demonstrating that even without overproduction they formed insoluble aggregates in the cell.
source: pRip, pSod2, and pMdh1 were present in the pellet fractions, demonstrating that even without overproduction they formed insoluble aggregates in the cell (Figure 1E).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in figures.

claim: pRip1 and pSod2 accumulated in the pam16-3 temperature-sensitive mutant.
source: pRip1 and pSod2 accumulated (Figure 1—figure supplement 1F) and consequently formed insoluble aggregates under these conditions (Figure 1F).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in figures.

claim: pRip1 and pSod2 formed insoluble aggregates in the pam16-3 temperature-sensitive mutant.
source: pRip1 and pSod2 accumulated (Figure 1—figure supplement 1F) and consequently formed insoluble aggregates under these conditions (Figure 1F).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in figures.

claim: The mistargeted precursor forms of mitochondrial proteins aggregated when their concentrations exceeded their solubility limits due to their overproduction.
source: Therefore, the mistargeted precursor forms of mitochondrial proteins aggregated, when their concentrations exceeded their solubility limits due to their overproduction, when the mitochondrial import defect was stimulated chemically, and when mutants of the presequence translocase import pathway were used.
evidence: This is stated as a conclusion from the current study's results.

claim: The mistargeted precursor forms of mitochondrial proteins aggregated when the mitochondrial import defect was stimulated chemically.
source: Therefore, the mistargeted precursor forms of mitochondrial proteins aggregated, when their concentrations exceeded their solubility limits due to their overproduction, when the mitochondrial import defect was stimulated chemically, and when mutants of the presequence translocase import pathway were used.
evidence: This is stated as a conclusion from the current study's results.

claim: The mistargeted precursor forms of mitochondrial proteins aggregated when mutants of the presequence translocase import pathway were used.
source: Therefore, the mistargeted precursor forms of mitochondrial proteins aggregated, when their concentrations exceeded their solubility limits due to their overproduction, when the mitochondrial import defect was stimulated chemically, and when mutants of the presequence translocase import pathway were used.
evidence: This is stated as a conclusion from the current study's results.

claim: pRip1 overexpression triggered small and rather specific transcriptomic changes, in which a total of nine genes were upregulated and four were downregulated.
source: pRip1 overexpression triggered small and rather specific transcriptomic changes, in which a total of nine genes (Figure 2C) were upregulated and four were downregulated (see also Figure 2A, Figure 2—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in figures.

claim: The KEGG enrichment analysis indicated that the oxidative phosphorylation pathway was upregulated for pRip1 overexpression.
source: The Kyoto Encyclopedia of Genes and Genomes (KEGG) enrichment analysis indicated that the oxidative phosphorylation pathway was upregulated, as expected, for pRip1 overexpression (Figure 2—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in figures.

claim: After 4 hr of pRip1 expression, the ATP-binding cassette (ABC) transporters appeared as the second most upregulated KEGG pathway.
source: After 4 hr of pRpi1 expression, the ATP-binding cassette (ABC) transporters appeared as the second most upregulated KEGG pathway (Figure 2—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in figures.

claim: For pRip1, the largest fold change was observed for the SSA1, SSA4, and HSP82 chaperones as a likely response to pRip1 aggregation.
source: For pRip1, the largest fold change was observed for the SSA1, SSA4, and HSP82 chaperones as a likely response to pRip1 aggregation (Figure 2A and C).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in figures.

claim: Extended pRip1 overproduction started to affect cellular performance as POT1, DLD3, AGP3, and PDC6 genes became downregulated.
source: Extended pRip1 overproduction started to affect cellular performance as the following genes became downregulated: POT1 (a peroxisomal protein that is also localized to the mitochondrial IM space and involved in fatty acid β-oxidation), DLD3 (involved in lactate biosynthesis), AGP3 (amino acid transmembrane transporter), and PDC6 (pyruvate decarboxylase) (Figure 2C).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in figures.

claim: The pam16-3 mutation had a stronger effect on the transcriptome than the effect of pRip1.
source: With regard to mitochondrial defects, the pam16-3 mutation had a stronger effect on the transcriptome than the effect of pRip1 (Figure 2—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in figures.

claim: Based on the KEGG analysis, oxidative phosphorylation-, metabolic pathway-, and citrate cycle-related genes were downregulated in the pam16-3 mutant.
source: Based on the KEGG analysis and as expected, oxidative phosphorylation-, metabolic pathway-, and citrate cycle-related genes were downregulated (Figure 2—figure supplement 1C).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in figures.

claim: More than half of the genes that were affected in the pam16-3 mutant encode mitochondrial proteins.
source: More than half of the genes that were affected encode mitochondrial proteins (Morgenstern et al., 2017; Figure 2—figure supplement 1D).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in figures and a citation.

claim: A group of genes that encode molecular chaperones was upregulated in the pam16-3 mutant.
source: Based on this analysis, we noticed that a group of genes that encode molecular chaperones was upregulated in the pam16-3 mutant (Figure 2D).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in figures.

claim: HSP82 and SSA4 were upregulated in the pam16-3 mutant, which were also upregulated in the case of pRip1 overexpression.
source: We observed the upregulation of HSP82 and SSA4, which were also upregulated in the case of pRip1 overexpression.
evidence: This is stated as an observation from the current study.

claim: SNO4, HSP26, HSP42, SSE2, HSP12, HSP32, HSP104, and HSP33 were upregulated in the pam16-3 mutant.
source: We also observed the upregulation of other molecular chaperone genes, including SNO4, HSP26, HSP42, SSE2, HSP12, HSP32, HSP104, and HSP33 (Figure 2B, blue, and Figure 2D).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in figures.

claim: The molecular chaperone response in pam16-3 went beyond the changes that were expected solely for the high-temperature treatment.
source: Our analysis showed that the molecular chaperone response in pam16-3 went beyond the changes that were expected solely for the high-temperature treatment.
evidence: This is stated as a result from the current study's analysis.

claim: The most pronounced changes in molecular chaperone expression were observed for SSE2, SIS1, HSP42, and HSP104 at 4 hr of treatment in the pam16-3 mutant.
source: The most pronounced changes were observed for SSE2, SIS1, HSP42, and HSP104 at 4 hr of treatment (Figure 2—figure supplement 1E, black arrows).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in figures.

claim: As the heat shock time was extended in the pam16-3 mutant, PDR5 gene levels changed, as well as other ABC transporter genes, including PDR15 and SNQ2.
source: The analysis of significantly altered genes showed that as the heat shock time was extended, PDR5 gene levels changed, as well as other ABC transporter genes, including PDR15 and SNQ2 (Figure 2—figure supplement 1F).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in figures.

claim: PDR5 is controlled by PDR3 transcription factor, the levels of which also increased in the pam16-3 mutant.
source: PDR5 is controlled by PDR3 transcription factor, the levels of which also increased (Gulshan et al., 2008).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to prior research.

claim: PDR5, PDR15, SNQ2, and PDR3 genes were shown to be involved in the mitochondrial compromised protein import response, mitoCPR response.
source: All of these genes were shown to be involved in the mitochondrial compromised protein import response, mitoCPR response (Weidberg and Amon, 2018).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to prior research.

claim: A significant response was observed for Hsp104 at the protein level when mitochondrial dysfunction was stimulated by CCCP.
source: We monitored changes in protein levels for all molecular chaperones against which we had antibodies available at the time of the studies, including Hsp104, Ssa1, Ssb1, Ssc1, Hsp60, and Edg1. No changes were observed for most of them, but a significant response was observed for Hsp104 (Figure 3A and B).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in figures.

claim: Hsp104 upregulation at the protein level was observed already after 15 min of CCCP treatment.
source: Notably, Hsp104 upregulation at the protein level was observed already after 15 min of treatment (Figure 3—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in figures.

claim: For all of the mutants under permissive conditions (19°C), Hsp104 was upregulated at the protein level.
source: For all of the mutants under permissive conditions (19°C; i.e., when only a mild protein import induction phenotype occurs), we observed the upregulation of Hsp104 at the protein level (Figure 3C).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in figures.

claim: Hsp42 abundance increased in response to CCCP treatment.
source: Consistent with the transcriptomic pam16-3 data, we observed an increase in the abundance of Hsp42 (Figure 3D).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in figures.

claim: Hsp104 levels were significantly upregulated upon metastable protein overproduction.
source: Hsp104 levels were significantly upregulated upon such protein overproduction (Figure 3E and F).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in figures.

claim: Hsp42 levels increased for all metastable proteins.
source: Here, we also observed an increase in the abundance of Hsp42 for all metastable proteins (Figure 3G and H).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in figures.

claim: In the case of pRip1, the Hsp42 response was not observed at the transcriptome level but was significant at the protein level.
source: In the case of pRip1, this response was not observed at the transcriptome level but was significant at the protein level (Figure 2C vs. Figure 3G and H).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in figures.

claim: The upregulation of specific molecular chaperones in response to cytosolic mitochondrial protein aggregation could be achieved both transcriptionally and post-transcriptionally.
source: Thus, the upregulation of specific molecular chaperones in response to cytosolic mitochondrial protein aggregation could be achieved both transcriptionally and post-transcriptionally.
evidence: This is stated as a conclusion from the current study's results.

claim: In the case of pRip1 overproduction, Hsp42 and Hsp104 were increased without any transcriptional stimulation.
source: Interestingly, in the case of pRip1 overproduction, Hsp42 and Hsp104 were increased without any transcriptional stimulation, meaning that in the case of mitochondrial precursor aggregates the post-transcriptional response can be uncoupled from transcription.
evidence: This is stated as an observation from the current study.

claim: Both Hsp42 and Hsp104 are molecular chaperones that are involved in aggregate handling in inclusion bodies.
source: In yeast, different types of aggregates have been identified (Sontag et al., 2017; Tyedmers et al., 2010). Both Hsp42 and Hsp104 are molecular chaperones that are involved in aggregate handling in inclusion bodies (Balchin et al., 2016; Mogk et al., 2015; Mogk et al., 2019).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior research.

claim: pRip1 accumulated in the form of inclusion body-like large deposits in the cytosol.
source: We observed the strong accumulation of pRip1 in the form of inclusion body-like large deposits in the cytosol (Figure 3I).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in figures.

claim: pRip1 deposits co-localized with Hsp42-GFP signals, indicating that Hsp42 sequestered pRip1 aggregates.
source: These deposits co-localized with the GFP signals, indicating that Hsp42 sequestered pRip1 aggregates.
evidence: This is stated as an observation from the current study.

claim: In cells with hsp104 deletion, there was an increase in the accumulation of pRip1 upon CCCP treatment.
source: In cells with hsp104 deletion, we observed an increase in the accumulation of pRip1 upon CCCP treatment (Figure 3J).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in figures.

claim: Hsp104 function was essential for limiting aggregates of mitochondrial precursors.
source: Thus, Hsp104 function was essential for limiting aggregates of mitochondrial precursors.
evidence: This is stated as a conclusion from the current study's results.

claim: Hsp104 was detected in the pellet fraction at higher amounts than without CCCP treatment, suggesting that an additional amount of Hsp104 associated with aggregates.
source: Based on the aggregation assay, we detected Hsp104 in the pellet fraction at higher amounts than without CCCP treatment, suggesting that an additional amount of Hsp104 associated with aggregates (Figure 3K).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in figures.

claim: The lack of Hsp42 did not result in the upregulation of pRip1, pSod2, or pMdh1.
source: The lack of Hsp42 did not result in the upregulation of pRip1, pSod2, or pMdh1 (Figure 3—figure supplement 2A and B).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in figures.

claim: The Δhsp42 strain exhibited the significant upregulation of Hsp104, suggesting a compensatory mechanism that diminishes negative consequences of Hsp42 deletion.
source: However, the Δhsp42 strain exhibited the significant upregulation of Hsp104, suggesting a compensatory mechanism that diminishes negative consequences of Hsp42 deletion (Figure 3L and M).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in figures.

claim: Hsp104 overproduction resulted in lower levels of pRip1, pSod2, and pMdh1 upon CCCP treatment.
source: Hsp104 overproduction resulted in lower levels of pRip1, pSod2, and pMdh1 upon CCCP treatment (Figure 3N, Figure 3—figure supplement 2C).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in figures.

claim: Higher levels of Hsp104 were associated with lower levels of Hsp42 in the cell.
source: In this case, we again observed a link between Hsp42 and Hsp104 levels, in which higher levels of Hsp104 were associated with lower levels of Hsp42 in the cell (Figure 3N, Figure 3—figure supplement 2D).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in figures.

claim: The overexpression of Hsp42 did not have an effect on pRip1, pSod2, or pMdh1 levels.
source: The overexpression of Hsp42 did not have such an effect on pRip1, pSod2, or pMdh1, in which levels of p forms did not change (Figure 3—figure supplement 2E and F).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in figures.

claim: Despite the beneficial effect of Hsp104 on precursor aggregate levels, no rescue of growth defects was observed for strains that expressed Atp2, Cox8, Cox12, pRip1, or Atp20 when either Hsp104 or Hsp42 was overproduced.
source: Despite the beneficial effect of Hsp104 on precursor aggregate levels, we did not observe the rescue of growth defects that were observed for strains that expressed Atp2, Cox8, Cox12, pRip1, or Atp20 when either Hsp104 or Hsp42 was overproduced (Figure 3—figure supplement 2G).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in figures.

claim: The aggregate-related chaperone response is activated in the cell to handle consequences of cytosolic accumulation of mitochondrial precursor proteins.
source: Altogether, our results show that the aggregate-related chaperone response is activated in the cell to handle consequences of cytosolic accumulation of mitochondrial precursor proteins.
evidence: This is stated as a conclusion from the current study's results.

claim: The overproduction of Atp2 and Cox8 resulted in the concurrent accumulation of other mitochondrial proteins, pRip1 and pSod2, in the total cell fractions.
source: The overproduction of Atp2 and Cox8 resulted in the concurrent accumulation of other mitochondrial proteins, pRip1 and pSod2, in the total cell fractions, without any other stimulation beyond just the overexpression of metastable proteins (Figure 4A–C, Figure 4—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in figures.

claim: Atp20 overproduction stimulated a significant increase in pSod2 but not pRip1 in the total cell fractions.
source: Atp20 overproduction also stimulated a significant increase in pSod2 but not pRip1 in the total cell fractions (Figure 4A–C).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in figures.

claim: Rip1, Sod2, and Mdh1 co-aggregated with Atp2 and Cox8 metastable proteins in the insoluble fraction.
source: Nevertheless, Rip1, Sod2, and Mdh1 co-aggregated with Atp2 and Cox8 metastable proteins in the insoluble fraction, based on the aggregation assay analysis (Figure 4D, Figure 4—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in figures.

claim: The greater abundance of aggregation-prone mitochondrial precursors resulted in the progression of mitochondrial protein import defect and consequently the larger cytosolic aggregation of mitochondrial precursors.
source: Thus, the greater abundance of aggregation-prone mitochondrial precursors resulted in the progression of mitochondrial protein import defect and consequently the larger cytosolic aggregation of mitochondrial precursors.
evidence: This is stated as a conclusion from the current study's results.

claim: The accumulation and aggregation of mitochondrial precursor proteins was partially counteracted by proteasome-mediated degradation.
source: Moreover, this process was partially counteracted by proteasome-mediated degradation. MG132-mediated protein inhibition led to an increase in the accumulation and aggregation of mitochondrial precursor proteins (Figure 4E, Figure 4—figure supplement 1C).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in figures.

claim: The average number of α-Syn aggregates per cell increased for pam16-3 at a permissive temperature of 19°C for both α-Syn WT-GFP and A53T-GFP compared with WT strain.
source: The average number of α-Syn aggregates per cell increased for pam16-3 at a permissive temperature of 19°C for both α-Syn WT-GFP and A53T-GFP compared with WT strain (Figure 4F and G, Figure 4—figure supplement 1D and E, Figure 4—source data 1a).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in figures.

claim: The increase in the average number of aggregates continued to grow for α-Syn WT-GFP at the restrictive temperature of 37°C.
source: The increase in the average number of aggregates continued to grow for α-Syn WT-GFP at the restrictive temperature of 37°C (Figure 4F).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in figures.

claim: The average number of α-Syn A53T-GFP aggregates was higher at 37°C than at the permissive temperature and did not significantly increase upon the mitochondrial import defect in the pam16-3 mutant.
source: The average number of α-Syn A53T-GFP aggregates was higher at 37°C than at the permissive temperature and did not significantly increase upon the mitochondrial import defect in the pam16-3 mutant (Figure 4G).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in figures.

claim: The A53T mutation of α-Syn resulted in larger aggregates compared with α-Syn WT.
source: The A53T mutation of α-Syn resulted in larger aggregates compared with α-Syn WT (Outeiro and Lindquist, 2003).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to prior research.

claim: There was no difference in the average size of aggregates for α-Syn WT at 19 and 37°C for both WT and pam16-3 mutant.
source: We did not observe any difference in the average size of aggregates for α-Syn WT at 19 and 37°C for both WT and pam16-3 mutant (Figure 4—figure supplement 1F, Figure 4—source data 1).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in figures.

claim: An increase in the average α-Syn A53T aggregate size was observed for WT and the pam16-3 mutant at 37°C when compared to 19°C.
source: We observed an increase in the average α-Syn A53T aggregate size for WT and the pam16-3 mutant at 37°C (Figure 4—figure supplement 1G, Figure 4—source data 1) when compared to 19°C.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in figures.

claim: For α-Syn A53T at 37°C the average number of aggregates did not significantly change after reaching a threshold and instead they were becoming larger as the aggregation progressed.
source: These findings suggest that for α-Syn A53T at 37°C the average number of aggregates did not significantly change after reaching a threshold and instead they were becoming larger as the aggregation progressed.
evidence: This is stated as an interpretation of the study's findings.

claim: Higher accumulation of pRip was observed at combined conditions of a pam16-3-stimulated mitochondrial import defect and α-Syn aggregation at 37°C.
source: Finally, we observed the higher accumulation of pRip at combined conditions of a pam16-3-stimulated mitochondrial import defect and α-Syn aggregation at 37°C (Figure 4H and I, Figure 4—figure supplement 1D and E).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in figures.
